newsitem.title: USA: Florida doctor defends assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: Florida doctor defends assisted suicide.

text.p: A doctor seeking the right to help terminally ill patients die said Wednesday he was prepared to help patients kill themselves if the practice was legal and seemed justified.
"I am prepared to write a prescription for the terminal patient and then get the drugs at the pharmacy for the patient," Dr. Cecil McIver told Palm Beach County Judge S. Joseph Davis.

McIver, 75, had testified in a right-to-die case Tuesday that he had never helped with a suicide, although he had been asked to do so during his 50 years as a doctor, because it would have broken the law.

He said he did not know what method he would use for assisting suicide. "I am not Dr. (Jack) Kevorkian," he said, referring to the Michigan doctor who has helped dozens of terminally ill people take their lives.

McIver is asking Davis for the right to help his patients die without facing manslaughter charges now applied to assisted suicide by Florida law. He was joined in the case by three patients, two of whom have since died.

Charles Hall, 34, the third patient, who is dying of AIDS, said he expected Davis to grant the request. "I think there is a very good chance the judge is going to look at the case closely and do the right thing. I think he has a good and kind heart," he told Reuters.

As McIver testified Wednesday, the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington heard arguments on whether to recognise a constitutional right for the terminally ill to get medical help in committing suicide. A decision is due by late June, when the Supreme Court completes its 1996-97 term.

McIver said he hoped Hall would never require his help in killing himself. But, he said, "indications are that Hall's condition is deteriorating. His viral count is quite high and his capacity to fight off disease is very low."
McIver's comments came during the third day of what was expected to be an eight-day trial.
